adapter: projects: rsi6/environments/projects.py with manifests/projects.json and data/projects/ (PSPLIB single-mode RCPSP, sets j30 and j60, 960 instances; activity lists decoded by the serial schedule-generation rule)
statement: Parsing, evaluation, relabelling and the hiding of the reference are correct in this adapter. In its current form it must not be used. On the 240 instances of the 24 classes with resource strength (RS) 1.0, the precedence-only earliest-start schedule already fits every capacity. The serial rule then turns every list in precedence order into exactly that schedule, so every valid answer scores 1. The kernel's split(env, 16, 24) puts two such classes (j30-8, j60-44) and one RS 0.7 class (j60-11) on the fresh side. That makes 17 of the 24 fresh instances, and the whole of half A, trivially solved. One random list in precedence order per fresh instance reaches the threshold of 0.9830 in 200 of 200 draws. Fix: leave out the instances whose earliest-start schedule fits, a rule that reads only the instance and removes exactly those 240. The new fresh side (j60-11, j60-2, j60-43; threshold 0.9864) is not reached by random lists (0 of 200 draws). It is still reached by the textbook latest-finish-time rule (0.9996), which the anchor must state. Apart from that, my own parser and serial-rule evaluator agree with the adapter on all 960 instances and all 960 reference values (862 optima, 98 upper bounds), on 400 valid and 160 out-of-order answers, and on partial evaluation. Changing the reference changes nothing the learner can observe. The training flag changes nothing. Relabelling removes the useful file order: the file-order list scores 0.949, the relabelled identity list 0. Malformed answers score 0. All ten pinned files re-fetch to the same hashes. The score scale is compressed, which the module text states correctly (random lists 0.914 on j30, 0.946 on j60). Two statements in the text are wrong. Some lists not in precedence order decode to valid schedules (they score 0 under the answer form's rule). And 46 of the 98 references called upper bounds equal the critical-path length printed in their own files, so they are optima.

findings.title: Every valid answer scores 1 on the 240 RS = 1.0 instances, which are 17 of the 24 fresh ones: random lists pass the threshold
findings.problem: In the 24 classes with resource strength (RS) 1.0 (classes 4, 8, ..., 48 of both sets, 240 instances), the capacities are at least the peak demand of the precedence-only earliest-start schedule. Under the serial rule, every list in precedence order then decodes to exactly that schedule. The proof is by induction along the list: an activity's predecessors finish at their earliest finish times, and beside the activities already placed it requests no more than in the earliest-start schedule, which fits. So every valid answer has makespan = critical-path length = reference and scores exactly 1; these instances measure nothing. split(env, 16, 24) puts j30-8 and j60-44 (both RS 1.0) and j60-11 (RS 0.7) on the fresh side. That makes 17 of the 24 fresh instances, and all of half A (j30-8, 9 instances), trivially solved. Any valid list therefore reaches the threshold on half A. On the whole fresh side, random lists in precedence order exceed the threshold 0.9830; the file-order list gets 0.9957, the earliest-start rule 0.9966 and the latest-finish-time (LFT) rule 1.0. On the training side, random lists get 0.927 against its threshold of 0.9765, so results would also look like generalisation from hard to easy instances. As built, parameter class 44 (NC 2.1, RF 0.75, RS 1.0) is on both sides (j30-44 training, j60-44 fresh). The module text names the fresh groups but not their RS. It gives random-list levels only over all 960 instances. And its anchor ('schedules five per cent longer than the reference') describes answers that cannot occur on 17 of the 24 fresh instances.
findings.evidence: c1.py printed 'RS=1.0 instances: 240 ESS resource-feasible: 240 ref == CP length: 240'. c8.py printed 'earliest-start schedule within capacities: 240 instances; all RS=1.0: True'. c6.py printed 'RS=1.0: 240 instances, 480 random valid lists, adapter scores: min 1.0 max 1.0', then 'fresh: mean of one random valid list per instance over 200 draws: min 0.9856 mean 0.9920; share >= threshold 0.9830: 1.000', then 'half A: ... 1.00', 'half B: ... 0.68'. c3.py printed 'fresh n=24 ... rand (0.9926, 3.06 % above ref) ... es 0.9966 ... lft 1.0 ... | RS=1.0: 17' and 'train n=16 ... rand 0.927 ... threshold 0.9765'. c10.py printed 'as built: ... parameter classes on both sides: [44]'.

findings.title: A one-pass textbook priority rule reaches the threshold on the fresh side, and the anchor does not say so
findings.problem: The latest-finish-time list reaches the threshold on the fresh side. It needs only a backward pass over the exposed durations and successor relation, with ties broken at random, decoded by the same serial rule. It scores 1.0 on all 24 fresh instances as built. After finding 1's fix it scores 0.9996 on the fresh side (threshold 0.9864), against 0.9529 on the training side (threshold 0.9726). Which three of the 96 classes form the fresh side is set by a hash order, and their difficulty differs widely. For example, grouping by class number across the two sets would put P29 and P9 (RS 0.2) on the fresh side, with threshold 0.9631. The anchor says only that random lists score high on this scale. A reader would take a pass as a capability beyond what a textbook rule achieves.
findings.evidence: c3.py printed 'fresh n=24 ... lft (1.0, 0.0) ... score==1: {es: 17, lft: 24}'. c8.py printed 'LFT rule: fresh 0.9996, training 0.9529 (threshold on training 0.9726)'. c10.py printed 'RS=1.0 left out, group = class number across sets: fresh groups [P29, P9] ... threshold 0.9631'.
findings.fix: In `anchor` and in the module text, state two numbers for the fresh side the kernel's split produces after finding 1's fix: the mean score of random lists in precedence order (0.970) and that of the latest-finish-time list under the serial rule (0.9996). Also state that the latter reaches the threshold, as jobshop's anchor does for textbook dispatching rules. If the operating point is meant to lie above a one-pass textbook rule, re-fix the threshold before any learner answer is scored on this category.

findings.title: Statement (5) and the text of group [2] are wrong: lists not in precedence order can decode to valid schedules
findings.problem: The module text says that a list not in precedence order 'is not a valid schedule', and that an activity placed before a predecessor gets a schedule that 'breaks a precedence relation'. Under the rule, such an activity can be pushed by the resources past the end of its predecessor. The decoded schedule then meets every published constraint, yet the hard group counts 1 and score() returns 0. The answer form's rule itself is consistent and visible to the learner, and nothing reachable is lost. But the text misstates what is invalid, and a report of 'invalid answers' would be misread as infeasible schedules.
findings.evidence: c7.py printed 'j309_4: activity 13 (job 15) listed before its direct predecessor 4 (job 6); decoded S[4]=10, d[4]=2, S[13]=41: S[13] >= S[4] + d[4] is True; whole schedule valid by my check; makespan 84 (reference 71); adapter score 0.0; evaluate() totals [84.0, 1177.0, 1.0]' and 'adjacent swaps of a predecessor and its successor tried: 3380; decoded schedule still valid: 726'.
findings.fix: Reword (5) and the description of group [2]: 'A list not in precedence order is not an answer of this form. The hard group counts every activity placed before one of its predecessors, and the score is 0, whether or not the schedule the rule gives breaks a precedence relation; it need not, since the resources may push the activity past its predecessor. Nothing reachable is lost: by (2), the list by start time of any valid schedule is in precedence order and denotes a schedule no longer.' No code change is needed.

findings.title: 46 of the 98 references labelled 'upper bound' equal their file's own critical-path length (MPM-Time) and are therefore optima
findings.problem: j60lb.sm gives no lower bounds for classes 42 to 48. For 46 instances in those classes, the reference equals the MPM-Time printed in the project line of the instance file. That is the critical-path length; my forward pass agrees on all 960 files. No schedule can be shorter, so these references are optima. Yet reference_kind returns 'upper bound', the module text says 'on the other 98 ... it is an upper bound only, and an answer can beat it', and the anchor speaks of 'the best known upper bound on the other 98'. Scores are unaffected, but reports by reference kind would be wrong for these 46.
findings.evidence: c12.py printed 'MPM-Time equals my critical-path length on 960 of 960' and ''upper bound' references: 98 ; equal to the critical-path length (hence optimal): 46 ; by class: {42: 5, 43: 9, 44: 10, 46: 2, 47: 10, 48: 10}'.
findings.fix: Either label a reference 'optimum' when it equals the file's MPM-Time (parsed in parse() and kept in the kernel-only instance table, never in the problem object), and change the text to '382 proven by the library, 46 more by the critical-path length, 52 upper bounds'; or keep the library's labels and say explicitly that 46 of the 98 cannot be beaten. After finding 1's fix, 26 such instances remain (classes 42, 43, 46, 47) among 78 upper-bound references.

evaluator_agreement:
My parser, decoder and feasibility check (own.py) share no code with the adapter.

- Instance tables: equal to the adapter's on all 960 instances (durations, requests, capacities, predecessor matrix, Z, group); 0 mismatches.
- References: parsed my own way from j30opt.sm (480 lines), j60hrs.sm (480) and j60lb.sm (410). They equal the adapter's values on all 960, and its kinds (862 optimum, 98 upper bound). The LB = UB count is 382, as the data page states, and no LB exceeds its UB. The JSON summaries agree with the text files; the j30 JSON upper bound equals the optimum on all 480.
- Valid answers: 400 random lists in precedence order on 20 instances (both sets, every RS level, training and fresh members). env.score equals my score 400/400. evaluate() totals [makespan, sum of finish times, out-of-order count] equal my decoder's 400/400. Every decoded schedule passes my independent precedence and per-period resource check. On RS = 1.0 instances every score is 1.
- Out-of-order answers: 160 random permutations. The totals (including the hard count) agree 160/160, and so do the scores.
- Partial evaluation: 24 random prefixes on 12 instances, half from valid lists and half from arbitrary permutations. totals() after every assign() equals partial_totals(). candidates() on the next position equals the slow rows from partial_totals(), and equals my own decoder's differences for every allowed option. candidates() on assigned and later positions equals the slow rows. The kernel test's loop also passes: 120 steps on 6 instances.
- score(decode(answer)) equals (Z - evaluate()[0]) / (Z - ref): 12/12.
- Reference answers: none to score. The source publishes values only; the heuristic upload format has start times, but the published solution files and JSON carry none.
exposed:
Every field the learner can see, traced to its source:
- n_vars = n_opts = J - 2 (30 or 60): the real jobs of the file.
- ordered = True: list positions are filled in index order. This is the adapter's answer form.
- capacity = ones(n): each activity is taken once, so a complete answer is a permutation.
- var_attr: shape (n, 0), nothing.
- opt_attr (n, 9), from REQUESTS/DURATIONS and RESOURCEAVAILABILITIES:
  - column 0: the duration d(j);
  - columns 1 to 4: the requests r(j, R 1..R 4);
  - columns 5 to 8: the capacities R(k), the same in every row.
  - Rows are permuted by the seed; the resource order is permuted by the seed, consistently in both column blocks.
- opt_opt[0] (n, n), from PRECEDENCE RELATIONS: 0/1, with [o, o'] = 1 when the line of o lists o' as a successor. Arcs from job 1 and to job J are dropped; the relation is directed and permuted with the rows.
- var_var, var_opt, occ_attr: empty.
- domain, start_answer, start_totals: None.
- hard = [F, F, T] and detail = [F, T, F], for three groups:
  - [0] the makespan of the placed prefix under the serial rule. For a complete list in precedence order this is the published objective.
  - [1] the sum of the finish times (detail). The instance does not state this; the rule computes it.
  - [2] the number of activities placed before a direct predecessor, i.e. the precedence constraint in list form.
- Never exposed (traced through the view and through pickles of the problem object): rel.date, duedate, tardcost, MPM-Time, horizon, base-data name, generator seed, class, instance number, reference. The reference value appears among the exposed numbers on 0 of 960 instances.

What the calls hand over: candidates() gives, for every unplaced activity, the makespan increase, its finish time under the rule, and whether a predecessor is missing. That is the eligible set plus the earliest resource-feasible finish of each candidate, the quantity a greedy earliest-finish rule uses. That greedy scores 0.935 on training and 0.920 on 120 other instances, below the LFT rule (0.968 on training), so it is not a solver in disguise.

Design decisions that shape difficulty:
- The serial decoding does the resource feasibility and left-justification. It makes every list in precedence order valid, and on the 240 RS = 1.0 instances it makes every valid list optimal (finding 1).
- The exact zero point Z (the sum of durations) compresses the scale: random valid lists score 0.914 on j30 and 0.946 on j60.
- The detail and hard groups hand over finish times and eligibility.

There is no search, ranking, pruning, optimisation call, or table beyond the instance.
